title: Furnishing & Interior Optimization for an Owned Property

slides.title: Buy for the guest and the safety list first. Style gets what is left.
slides.subtitle: Lesson OP.6. Furnishing & Interior Optimization for an Owned Property
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, fire code, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
This lesson turns a furnishing budget into a purchase plan for one specific house. By the end you'll have a room-by-room plan that matches a named guest. You'll have a sleeping layout the listing can state truthfully, and a safety list you can show your insurer and fire marshal.

You'll also leave with a delivery schedule, a linen cycle, a locked owner closet, and a replacement estimate. The last piece is a room inventory. That sheet goes to Sam, who records the course's live demos. In his OP.1 lesson he builds the listing on each booking site.

We'll use Cedar Ridge the whole way through. Maya and Chris are the couple buying Cedar Ridge, the lake house in our running example. They set a $32,000 furnishing budget in the underwriting. My job here is to show you how they spend it well, in the right order, without finding more money. All the Cedar Ridge figures are hypothetical and marked that way.

slides.title: Write down who books the house before you open a single catalog

left.head: The guest profile
left.note: Four parts; read complaints in reviews of similar nearby listings (Sam's PA.4 package)
items: Who comes
How many sleep over
What they do all day
What they complain about at comparable houses

right.head: What each profile demands
right.note: Then list what the house is not for, like parties
items: Families: a table for everyone, a crib that meets current standards, furniture that can't tip
Work groups: a real desk and reliable internet
Lake crowd: towels you don't mind seeing on a dock
Stairs only to the lower level? Don't imply step-free access

slides.notes:
Most furnishing mistakes start in a store. Someone falls for a sofa, then makes the house fit the sofa. I want you to reverse that.

Write down who books this house and what they'll do there. Then buy for that person. The profile has four parts. The fourth one, complaints, comes from reading reviews of similar nearby listings, the comparable set. They're in the underwriting package Sam walks through in PA.4. If you skipped that, pick three similar listings nearby. Their reviews tell you what guests in this market already dislike.

Then write the other list: what this house is not for. If you won't allow parties, you don't need a sound system. If the lower level only has stairs, you can't imply step-free access.

Every accessibility claim has to be true on the day a guest arrives. Airbnb's ground rules for hosts say the listing should describe the home and the amenities available from check-in to checkout. So the guest profile also protects you from promising things the house can't deliver.

slides.title: Set the sleeping layout before you buy, and count it by bed, not by room
items: The layout drives bookings, linen count, cleaning time, and insurance
If your guest count depends on a sofa bed, say so plainly in the listing
Airbnb counts a bunk as 2 beds, so list bed types next to the guest count
Check 1: occupancy limits and permit conditions on guest count (PA.9)
Check 2: egress, a way out in a fire from each bedroom, that officials accept
Check 3: insurance, because a mismatched guest count can create a claim problem
slides.notes:
Guests check the sleeping layout twice. It's the one number they read closely, because it decides whether their group fits. It also sets your linen count and how long every turnover takes.

So I set it first, before any purchase. And I count sleeping spots by bed. Six beds can mean six people or twelve, depending on whether they're twins or queens. So list the bed types and the guest count together.

Airbnb's sleeping arrangements article says a bunk bed counts as 2 beds in the bed count on the listing. Keep that in mind when you read the Cedar Ridge numbers in a minute.

Before you lock the layout, run three checks. Occupancy limits and permit conditions should already be in your PA.9 due diligence notes. If not, ask the licensing office. Egress means a way out in a fire. Every sleeping room needs one that your building or fire official accepts, so ask them what counts. And insurance: if the policy says one guest count and the listing says another, that gap can become a claim problem. Settle all three before the bunk beds get ordered.

slides.title: Work space, storage, and outdoor gear get skipped in budgets, then show up in reviews

left.head: Work space and storage
items: A workspace is a desk, chair, lamp, and outlets within reach
If the internet can't hold a video call, don't advertise remote work
Test the speed at the desk; write it down for the listing and the handoff packet
Guests need space for a suitcase and clothes; the owner needs a locked closet

right.head: Outdoor use
items: Lake houses earn their rate outside, and many injuries happen there
A grill needs cleaning, fuel checks, and a placement your insurer accepts
A fire pit, dock, kayak, or hot tub each carries its own insurance question
If you can't maintain it every turnover, don't list it

slides.notes:
Three areas get left out of most furnishing budgets. Then they appear in reviews.

The first is the work space. If you claim a dedicated workspace, a guest expects a desk, a chair, a lamp, and outlets they can reach. And the internet has to hold a video call. Test the speed at the desk itself, not in the kitchen. Write the result in your handoff packet, the property reference file from PA.12.

The second is storage, and it means two things. Guests need somewhere to put a suitcase and hang clothes for a four-night stay. The owner needs a locked place for personal items, spare inventory, and cleaning stock. Mix those two and you get the classic review: closets full of the owner's stuff.

The third is outdoor use. A lake house earns its rate on the deck and the water. That's also where many injuries happen. Every outdoor item is a maintenance job and an insurance question. If you can't keep it right every turnover, meaning the clean and reset between stays, leave it out of the listing.

slides.title: Safety equipment is the first line in the budget, and CPSC guidance sets the floor
slides.text: Airbnb: say whether smoke and CO (carbon monoxide) alarms are present, and keep them working. The CPSC (Consumer Product Safety Commission) list is a planning floor, not your code.
items: Smoke alarms: every level, outside each sleeping area, every bedroom
CO alarms: every level, outside sleeping areas
At least one fire extinguisher
TVs and furniture anchored; no dangling cords
Pools, spas: compliant drain covers; fence at least 4 feet, self-closing, self-latching gates
Cribs meet CPSC standards; bare sleep space
Cleaning supplies locked or out of reach
Recall check at SaferProducts.gov
slides.notes:
Safety goes first in the budget, not last. Nothing gets cut from this layer later.

Airbnb's safety requirements say hosts must state whether smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are present. If they are, they must work and you must test them regularly. The same page says you must deal with fire and electrical hazards. That covers blocked exits, dead smoke detectors, exposed wiring, and poorly kept hot tubs, gas appliances, and furnaces. You're responsible for any area guests can use.

The checklist on this slide comes from the Consumer Product Safety Commission's vacation rental safety tips. It covers alarms, extinguishers, anchoring, pools, cribs, and cleaning supplies.

This is consumer guidance, and your local code may ask for more. Your city, county, or state may require more, such as alarms that are wired to each other. So I treat this list as a planning floor, and I ask the fire marshal what this address needs.

slides.title: Cameras stay outside and disclosed, and nothing that records goes indoors
rows: Allowed if the listing discloses its location; can't point into the house or cover private areas like an enclosed outdoor shower
Doorbell camera, outside, location written into the listing
Allowed in common spaces if it measures sound level only and is disclosed; not in bedrooms, bathrooms, or sleeping areas
slides.caption: Source: Airbnb help article 3061 on cameras and devices. Policies change; recheck before you publish.
slides.notes:
Security devices come next, because they touch privacy and listing accuracy at the same time.

Airbnb's device rules ban security cameras and recording devices that monitor indoor spaces. That holds even if the device is turned off. Hidden cameras are prohibited everywhere.

Exterior cameras are allowed, with conditions. The listing has to disclose where they are. They can't point into the house. And they can't cover areas where people expect more privacy, like an enclosed outdoor shower or a sauna.

Noise monitors that only measure sound level are allowed in common spaces. They have to be disclosed, and they stay out of bedrooms, bathrooms, and sleeping areas.

So at Cedar Ridge the plan is simple. If Maya and Chris want a camera, they buy a doorbell camera. It goes outside, and its location goes into the listing. The noise monitor sits in a common area and gets disclosed. Check Airbnb's current page before you publish, since these rules change.

slides.title: Every item has three prices: purchase, turnover minutes, and replacement
items: Buy performance (stain-resistant) or washable fabrics for the living room
Put waterproof encasements on every mattress on day one
Buy white or one-color bedding from one product line, so sets mix and match
Choose dishware you can rebuy by the piece, and keep spares on a shelf
Skip glass tabletops and lamps that need an app to turn on

box.label: Why minutes cost money
box.text: Twelve decorative pillows add minutes to every turnover, and the cleaner is paid per turnover.

slides.notes:
Every item you buy has three prices. There's the purchase price. There's the minutes it adds to each turnover. And there's the cost of replacing it. The cheapest sofa is often the most expensive one by year three.

These buying rules hold up. Washable fabrics and removable covers let the cleaner handle a spill without a service call. Encasements go on every mattress on the first day. A stained mattress is a replacement. A stained encasement is a wash.

White or one-color bedding from one product line means any sheet fits any bed of that size. Dishware you can rebuy by the piece means one broken plate doesn't mean a new set.

Then think in cleaning minutes. Twelve decorative pillows get fluffed and placed after every stay. The cleaner is paid per turnover, not per hour. So extra minutes either get rushed or show up later as a higher rate. Buy for the turnover, not the photo.

slides.title: Build the $32,000 plan in five layers, and never cut safety, mattresses, or linens
slides.keyline: The budget is fixed by the underwriting. Your job is to spend it well, not find more.

nodes.d: Plus encasements. They carry the listing and the reviews
3 sets per bed; 3 towel sets per guest
Bed frames, dressers, kitchen, dining, living, work, outdoor

box.label: Contingency and tax note
box.text: Hold a 3-5% contingency on top of the five layers (assumption). Over budget? Cut layers 4 and 5 first. The CPA decides how each item is treated for tax.

slides.notes:
The furnishing budget is a fixed input from the underwriting. Maya and Chris set $32,000 for Cedar Ridge. Your job is to spend it well, not to find more.

I build the plan in five layers, in this order. Safety and access come first, and nothing gets cut there. Mattresses and their encasements come second, because the beds carry the listing and the reviews. Linens come third, sized to a cycle: three sheet sets per bed, one on the bed, one in the wash, one on the shelf. Towels follow guests, three sets per guest.

Layer four is room furniture and decor. That includes bed frames and dressers, plus the kitchen, dining, living room, work space, and deck. Layer five is delivery, assembly, spares, and owner storage. On top of that, hold a contingency of 3 to 5% of the budget.

When you're over budget, you cut from layers four and five. On tax treatment of the furnishings, the CPA makes the call.

slides.title: Cedar Ridge sleeps 8 on 6 beds, and no sofa bed is needed to get there
slides.text: Three bedrooms, two baths, lake market, no HOA (no homeowners' association rules). Expected year: 61 stays of about 3.5 nights. The owners use it about 10 days a year.

box.label: Guest profile (assumption)
box.text: Two related families or two couples with kids. Friday arrival, lake days, most dinners cooked in. Midweek shoulder season: remote workers and small groups. No parties, no pets at launch.

slides.notes:
Cedar Ridge is a three-bedroom, two-bath house in a drive-to lake market. It sleeps 8 and has no homeowners' association. In a normal year, our base case, it expects 61 stays at about 3.5 nights each.

The assumed floor plan has a main level with the kitchen, dining, living room, primary bedroom, and bath 1. A walkout lower level holds bedroom 2, a bunk room, and bath 2. A deck faces the lake.

The layout gets to 8 without a sofa bed. The king sleeps 2. The queen sleeps 2. The two bunks sleep 4. On the listing, that shows as 6 beds, because each bunk counts as 2.

Every bed type is listed exactly as installed. So the listing never depends on someone agreeing to sleep on a couch.

The guest profile matches the house. Two families, or two couples with kids, doing lake days and cooking dinner. Midweek in shoulder season, the months between peak and off-peak, brings some remote workers and small groups. That's why the plan includes a work nook.

slides.title: The first draft ran $1,565 over, so layers 4 and 5 absorbed $2,760 in cuts
slides.side:
Layers 1-3 (safety, mattresses, linens) stayed untouched.

Layer 4 gave $2,360: sectional $400, accent chairs $300, outdoor dining $250, bed frames and dressers $650, and smaller items. Layer 5 gave $400: the owners assemble small items.
slides.notes:
The first draft of the room-by-room plan came to $33,565. That's $1,565 over the $32,000 budget, with no contingency at all. So we cut before buying anything.

Look at where the cuts came from. Layers one to three, safety, mattresses, and linens, stayed untouched. Layer four, room furniture and decor, gave $2,360. The sectional dropped from $2,400 to $2,000. The bed frames and dressers gave $650 together. The accent chairs, TV, rug, art, and outdoor furniture each gave up $100 to $300. Layer five gave $400, because the owners assemble small items themselves.

Thirteen cuts added up to $2,760. That brings final purchases to $30,805. The budget minus purchases leaves a contingency of $1,195. That's about 3.7% of the budget.

This is the cut rule from the five layers in action. When the draft is over, you cut room furniture and logistics before safety, mattresses, or linens. And if contingency falls below 3%, you cut again before ordering.

slides.title: The living room is the largest room line at $5,220, and every tall piece is anchored
rows: King frame and mattress, encasement, anchored dresser, blackout curtains
Queen frame and mattress, encasement, anchored dresser
2 bunk frames ($1,300), 4 twin mattresses ($1,200), anchored dresser
Performance-fabric sectional, TV with mount or anti-tip strap
Cookware, dishes and glassware for 12, coffee makers
Hair dryers, mats, curtains, bins, mirrors
Outdoor dining set, 4 lounge chairs, gas grill, path lighting
slides.caption: All figures are assumptions from OP.6.7. Linens, safety, storage, and logistics are on the next slide.
slides.notes:
This is the final plan for the rooms. I've shortened the item lists to fit, but the amounts are the ones in the lesson.

A few things to notice. Every bedroom dresser is anchored. The TV has a mount or an anti-tip strap. That's the CPSC anchoring guidance showing up as a line item, not an afterthought.

The bunk room is the most expensive bedroom, at $3,920. Two twin-over-twin frames cost $1,300, and four twin mattresses cost $1,200. Those four beds carry half the guest count, so they get real mattresses.

The living room is the biggest single line, at $5,220. It gets a performance-fabric sectional, because that's where spills happen.

The kitchen is stocked for 12, not 8. Dishes break and get used between dishwasher runs. And the work nook is only $510, but it's what lets Maya and Chris honestly claim a workspace for the midweek guests. The next slide covers the layers that aren't rooms.

slides.title: Linens, safety, storage, and logistics close the plan at exactly $32,000
rows: Sheets, duvets, pillows, bath and lake towels
5 smoke alarms, 3 CO alarms, 3 extinguishers, first aid kit, anti-tip kits, smart lock, doorbell camera, noise monitor
Unspent balance moves to the breakage reserve
slides.caption: Alarm count follows CPSC placement for this layout: 3 bedrooms + 1 outside sleeping areas per level. The fire marshal may change it.
slides.notes:
The rest of the plan covers the layers that aren't rooms.

Linens and towels come to $4,005. I'll build that number step by step in two slides.

Safety and access is $1,280. It includes three extinguishers, which I assumed go in the kitchen, the lower level, and near the grill. The alarm count follows the CPSC placement guidance for this assumed layout. There's one smoke alarm in each of the three bedrooms. Then there's one outside the sleeping areas on each level. That's five. There's one CO alarm on each level outside sleeping areas, plus one near the furnace. That's three. The fire marshal may change those counts, and the fire marshal wins.

Owner storage and spares is $950. Launch logistics is $1,900.

All of that brings purchases to $30,805. The contingency of $1,195 isn't spent at launch. If it's still unspent, it moves into a separate breakage account. The total lands on $32,000 exactly, the number from the underwriting.

slides.title: In the exercise's five layers, the plan spends $30,805 and holds $1,195 back
rows: Alarms, extinguishers, first aid, lock, camera, monitor
The linen cycle on the next slide
Everything else in the rooms, kitchen, baths, and deck
Held back; unspent money seeds the breakage account
slides.caption: Same plan as the two previous slides, regrouped into the layers you fill in for OP.6.9.
slides.notes:
Here's the same Cedar Ridge plan, regrouped into the five layers. This is the shape you'll fill in for your own house in the exercise, so I want you to see a finished one.

Layer one, safety and access, is $1,280. Layer two, mattresses and encasements, is $3,870. That's $2,300 for the king and queen mattresses, $1,200 for the four twins, and $370 for six encasements. Layer three, linens and towels, is $4,005, and I'll build that number next.

Layer four, room furniture and decor, is the big one at $18,800. That's every frame, dresser, table, chair, rug, and lamp, plus the kitchen, the baths, and the deck. Layer five, logistics, storage, and spares, is $2,850.

Those five add up to $30,805 in purchases. The $1,195 contingency sits on top, and the total lands on $32,000. Notice where the cuts landed: all in layers four and five.

slides.title: Three sets per bed and three towel sets per guest put linens at $4,005

lines.label: Duvet inserts, 1 per bed plus a spare king
Kitchen towels and extra bath mats

slides.side:
61 stays × 6 beds = 366 sheet-set changes a year.

Spread over 18 sets, each set is washed about 20 times a year. Replace on a rolling basis, not all at once.
slides.notes:
The linen cycle sets how much bedding you buy. So I build the number from the cycle, not from a guess.

Six beds at three sheet sets each is 18 sets. The king sets run $90, the queen $75, and the twins $45. That's $1,035. Duvet covers follow the same three-per-bed rule for $870. Inserts are one per bed plus a spare king, $580.

Pillows are four on the king, four on the queen, and one per twin. That's 12, plus 4 spares, so 16 at $25. Add 16 protectors at $10, so $160.

Towels follow guests, not beds. A set here is a bath towel, a hand towel, and a washcloth. Eight guests times three sets is 24 sets at $25, so $600. Then two lake towels per guest, 16 at $15, so $240, and kitchen towels and extra mats at $120.

Now look at the wear. With 61 stays and all six beds stripped each time, that's 366 sheet-set changes a year. Across 18 sets, each set gets washed about 20 times a year. Plan to replace linens on a rolling basis.

slides.title: Replacing furnishings costs about $5,982 a year, about $98 per stay
rows: TV, lock, doorbell camera, noise monitor
Case goods (hard furniture), upholstery, rugs, decor
slides.caption: Lives are planning assumptions, not tax lives.
slides.notes:
New furniture doesn't fail on schedule, but it does wear out. So I spread each group over an assumed replacement life. These are planning lives, not tax lives.

The groups trace back to the plan. Linens are the $4,005 linen plan plus six encasements. Smallwares are the kitchen and bathrooms. Mattresses are the king, queen, and four twins. Case goods, meaning dressers, tables, frames, and other hard furniture, cover the rest of the rooms. Delivery, assembly, consumables, and storage are left out.

The total is $5,982 a year, about $98 per stay. The operating budget sets aside 5% of gross for repairs and 5% for a capital reserve, $7,428 together. Furniture wear alone would use about 81% of it. The repairs line alone doesn't cover it. Take that question to Sam's OP.10 review.

One more rule: any single replacement over $200 needs owner approval. That's an assumption; OP.8 builds it into the cleaning SOP.

box.label: Is the reserve enough?
box.text: Cedar Ridge's plan sets aside 5% for repairs and 5% for capital items, $7,428 a year together. Furniture wear alone would use about 81% of it. Take that to OP.10.

slides.title: Setup runs 21 days from possession, and the test stay is the step people skip
rows: Order long-lead items (sectional, mattresses, bunks) for Day 3 or later; keep orders reschedulable
Change locks, smart lock, smoke and CO alarms, extinguishers, first aid; safety walk; deep clean
Beds, bunks, dressers assembled; tall furniture anchored
Living and dining furniture, TV mount, work nook
Doorbell camera and noise monitor installed; locations noted for the listing
Kitchen and linens stocked; owner closet locked; spares labeled
Test stay: the owners sleep there and use every item
Punch list: fix what the test stay found; first full clean to the OP.8 standard
Photos; room inventory handed to Sam's OP.1 setup
slides.notes:
Day 0 is possession after closing, from PA.11. Photo day is Day 21. Every step in between has a name on it.

The long-lead items get ordered before closing. The sectional, the mattresses, and the bunks can take weeks. They're set to arrive on Day 3 or later, after the locks are changed and the house is clean. Order only what you can reschedule, in case closing moves.

Beds go in before living room furniture, because beds carry the listing. Tall furniture gets anchored the same day it's assembled. Alarms, extinguishers, and the first aid kit go in during the first two days, before any crew arrives. The camera and noise monitor come on days 10 to 12, and their locations go into the listing.

The step people skip is the test stay on days 16 and 17. Maya and Chris sleep there and use every item. That's how you find the missing shower hook and the blind that won't close.

The owner closet gets locked on days 13 to 15. It holds personal items for their 10 personal-use days, spares, and cleaning stock. Only the owners and the cleaner have the code.

slides.title: Photograph the house exactly as a guest will find it, because Airbnb can check
slides.text: Run this the evening before photo day.
items: Every bed made in the standard set the cleaner will use
Every lamp working; surfaces cleared of anything a guest won't find
Safety equipment in place; extinguishers easy to reach; alarm locations noted
Doorbell camera location photographed; no camera indoors
Owner closet locked; no personal items in guest areas
Outdoor furniture set up; grill clean and covered
One shot of each bed type, so the layout is visible
Work nook set up; internet speed result saved
slides.notes:
Airbnb's search page says quality is a major factor in how listings appear. Quality includes photos and videos, ratings and reviews, host communication, and listing characteristics. Guests can also filter by amenities. An amenity you have but don't list can't show in a filtered search. An amenity you list but don't have becomes an accuracy problem.

Airbnb can also ask hosts to confirm photo accuracy by taking new photos in person through the app. So the photos have to match the house a guest will walk into.

This checklist runs the evening before photos. Beds are made the way the cleaner will make them every time. The bunk detail shot shows the layout. The doorbell camera location gets photographed for the disclosure.

Then fill in the room inventory. That's the next slide. Sam's OP.1 lesson turns that sheet into the listing on each booking site. Your job is to hand him facts that are true and complete.

slides.title: Hand Sam one row per room, with only facts that are true on arrival day
slides.caption: Sample rows from Cedar Ridge; the full sheet lists every room. Sam's OP.1 lesson turns it into the listing.
slides.notes:
This is the room inventory, the last thing this lesson promised you. It's one row per room, and every cell has to be true on the day a guest arrives.

For each room, write the beds or seating, the amenities you'll list, and the safety items in that room. Then add the photo shots you need and any notes for the listing text. These are three sample rows from Cedar Ridge. The full sheet lists every room, including the kitchen, the baths, and the work nook.

Look at the notes column. The bunk room says lower level, stairs only. That's the accessibility claim from the guest profile, written down so nobody promises step-free access by mistake. The deck row notes the grill rules and an extinguisher nearby, if the fire marshal agrees.

Sam's OP.1 lesson turns this sheet into the listing on each booking site. Your job is to hand him facts that are true and complete.

slides.title: Fill in the five layers before ordering, and cut layers 4 and 5 first if you're over
rows: 3. Linens and towels (3 per bed, 3 towel sets per guest)
4. Room furniture and decor (frames, dressers, kitchen, living, outdoor)
slides.caption: Rules: over budget, cut layers 4 and 5 before layers 1-3. Contingency under 3%, cut again. Replacement pace above your repairs line, flag it for OP.10. A claim you can't verify on site stays out of the listing.
slides.notes:
This is Part B of the exercise. Part A comes first in the lesson. It covers your guest profile and what the house is not for. It also covers the maximum occupancy at your address, your bed list, and the accessibility features you measured on site.

Then build the budget in the same five layers you just saw for Cedar Ridge. The total has to equal the furnishing budget from your underwriting. Fill in the budget column first. Then get real quotes and fill in the actual column. The variance shows where the plan drifted.

The decision rules are in the box. If the draft is over budget, cut layers four and five before you touch safety, mattresses, or linens. If contingency drops below 3%, cut again before you order anything.

If your replacement pace is bigger than your repairs line, flag it for Sam's OP.10 review. To estimate your pace, copy the Cedar Ridge table: group your purchases, give each group a life, divide. And if you can't verify a claim on site, it stays out of the listing.

box.label: Decision rules
box.text: Over budget: cut layers 4 and 5 first. Contingency under 3%: cut again. Replacement pace above your repairs line: flag for OP.10. Can't verify a claim on site: leave it out.

slides.title: Four offices and Airbnb's help pages confirm what you can't decide alone
rows: Maximum occupancy, bedroom egress, permit conditions tied to beds or guest count
Smoke and CO alarm type, placement, interconnection, and extinguisher needs for this address
Listed guest count, bunk beds, grill, fire features, water access, any pool or hot tub
How furnishings, linens, supplies, delivery, and assembly are classified; whether the 5-year treatment holds
Device rules and listing accuracy, checked again before publishing
slides.notes:
A furnishing plan looks like shopping. But parts of it are someone else's decision: four offices, plus Airbnb's own help pages.

The licensing office or building department confirms maximum occupancy, bedroom egress, and any permit condition tied to beds or guest count. If they say six, the bunk room plan changes.

The fire marshal confirms alarm type, placement, interconnection, and extinguishers. The CPSC list we used is a floor. The marshal sets the actual count for this address.

The insurer confirms the listed guest count, the bunks, the grill, fire features, water access, and any pool or hot tub. Bring the room inventory to that call.

The CPA confirms how furnishings, linens, supplies, delivery, and assembly are classified. Ask whether treating the full $32,000 as 5-year property, as the Cedar Ridge illustration does, holds for your purchases.

And Airbnb's help pages change. Check the device rules and listing accuracy pages again right before you publish.

slides.title: This week, turn your furnishing budget into a plan for one real address
items: Read reviews of 3 comparable listings; write your guest profile
Call the licensing office for max occupancy; write your bed list
Fill in the five-layer budget; check contingency is at least 3%
Ask the fire marshal which alarm placement this address needs
slides.next: Next: OP.7 Building Your Ops Team: Cleaner, Co-Host, or Property Manager. It decides who cleans, restocks, inspects, answers guests, and approves spending like the $200 replacement limit.
slides.notes:
Four actions this week.

Start with the guest. Pull three comparable listings from your PA.4 package and read their reviews. Write down who books, how many sleep over, what they do, and what they complain about. Then write what your house is not for.

Next, call the licensing office. Ask for the maximum occupancy at your address and any permit condition on guest count. Then write your bed list by room and type.

Third, open the five-layer budget and put in your underwriting number. Rough in each layer and check that contingency is at least 3%.

Fourth, ask the fire marshal's office about alarm placement for your address.

The house is furnished and the listing facts are ready. Now someone has to keep it that way after every stay. That's OP.7. It decides who cleans, restocks, inspects, answers guests, and holds a key. It also decides who can approve spending, like the $200 replacement limit we set here. Any single replacement over $200 needs owner approval, and OP.8 writes that into the SOP.
